evidence.claim: A long, narrow valley links Pikeville, Dunlap, Whitwell and Jasper
evidence.quote: The Tennessee section of Sequatchie Valley contains the towns of Pikeville, Dunlap, Whitwell, Jasper

evidence.claim: The Sequatchie Valley National Scenic Byway follows a rolling valley bordered by mountains, a 70-mile drive in the byway organization’s description.
evidence.quote: The Sequatchie Valley National Scenic Byway offers 70 miles of rolling valley bordered by beautiful mountains

evidence.claim: The valley itself is almost perfectly straight, with a width of about three to five miles.
evidence.quote: From its northern end to its geological southern end at Browns Valley, the valley is almost perfectly straight.

evidence.claim: Tennessee’s Department of Transportation identifies scenic and recreational qualities as the basis for this National Scenic Byway, emphasizing the landscape and opportunities for hiking, fishing and wildlife watching.
evidence.quote: INTRINSIC QUALITIES Scenic / Recreational

evidence.claim: Travel through the valley mattered before the present highway. During the Civil War, a rough route through it supplied the Union army at Chattanooga.
evidence.quote: A rough travel route through the Sequatchie Valley was the only available route to provide food and supplies to the Union army in Chattanooga.

evidence.claim: At Crossville, a branch of the Great Stage Road met the Kentucky Stock Road, a cattle-driving route that eventually extended south to Chattanooga.
evidence.quote: Crossville developed at the intersection of a branch of the Great Stage Road, which connected the Knoxville area with the Nashville area, and the Kentucky Stock Road, a cattle drovers' path connecting Middle Tennessee with Kentucky and later extending south to Chattanooga.

evidence.claim: Those roads were widened, improved and paved; U.S. 70 and U.S. 127 now roughly follow the old routes.
evidence.quote: The roads were gradually widened, improved and turned into paved roads. Two major federal highways—U.S. Route 70, which traverses Tennessee from east to west, and U.S. Route 127, which traverses Tennessee from north to south—now roughly follow the old routes.

evidence.claim: Drive north from Jasper on TN 28 through Whitwell to Dunlap, then continue on U.S. 127 toward Pikeville.
evidence.quote: Continue on TN-28 through Jasper, Whitwell, and Dunlap, Tennessee. TN-28 becomes US-127 in Dunlap, Tennessee. Proceed north through Pikeville and Crossville, Tennessee.

evidence.claim: At Dunlap, the coke ovens lie at the foot of Fredonia Mountain west of downtown.
evidence.quote: The Dunlap Coke Ovens are situated at the base of Fredonia Mountain, along a stream known as Coops Creek.  The ovens and surrounding park are located on Mountain View Road, just under a mile west of downtown Dunlap.

evidence.claim: Beyond Pikeville, U.S. 127 climbs toward Crossville on the plateau.
evidence.quote: The primary highway running through Pikeville is U.S. Route 127, which connects the city to Crossville atop the plateau to the north and Dunlap to the south.

evidence.claim: The driving itinerary finishes at I-40 in Crossville.
evidence.quote: End at I-40 in Crossville, Tennessee (mile marker 322).

evidence.claim: a width of about three to five miles
evidence.quote: Its width is about 3–5 miles (5–8 km).

evidence.claim: opportunities for hiking, fishing and wildlife watching
evidence.quote: These areas provide many opportunities for hiking, camping, picnicking, hunting, fishing, bird watching, and wildlife viewing.

evidence.claim: A German transport railcar surrounded by a small garden forms Whitwell’s Children’s Holocaust Memorial.
evidence.quote: The Children's Holocaust Memorial consists of an authentic German transport car (which arrived in the Baltimore seaport on September 9, 2001) surrounded by a small garden.

evidence.claim: Its 11 million paper clips grew out of a school project begun in 1998.
evidence.quote: The railcar is filled with 11 million paper clips

evidence.claim: Principal Linda M. Hooper asked for an after-school project to teach tolerance, and David Smith and Sandra Roberts developed a Holocaust education program.
evidence.quote: In 1998, Linda M. Hooper, principal of Whitwell Middle School in Whitwell, Tennessee, asked Assistant Principal David Smith to find a voluntary after-school project to teach the children about tolerance. David Smith and Sandra Roberts started a Holocaust education program

evidence.claim: Students sought objects that could represent lives lost in the Holocaust, choosing paper clips after researching Norwegian resistance to Nazi occupation.
evidence.quote: Through Internet research, David Smith discovered that Norwegians wore paperclips on their lapels during World War II as a silent protest against Nazi occupation.

evidence.claim: The memorial was unveiled on November 9, 2001, the anniversary of Kristallnacht.
evidence.quote: The monument was unveiled on the anniversary of the Kristallnacht, November 9, 2001.

evidence.claim: Students sought objects that could represent lives lost in the Holocaust
evidence.quote: asked Mrs. Hooper if they could collect something to represent the lives that were exterminated during the Holocaust.

evidence.claim: Five batteries of 268 beehive ovens remain at Dunlap’s former coke works.
evidence.quote: the facility consists of five batteries of 268 beehive ovens

evidence.claim: Coal from Fredonia Mountain traveled down an incline railway and into openings atop the ovens.
evidence.quote: An incline railway connected the ovens to a coal mine further up the mountain slope, and railroad cars would carry coal from the mine to the tops of the batteries and dump the coal into the ovens' top openings.

evidence.claim: Workers heated it in closed chambers to remove volatile material, producing coke for Chattanooga’s iron furnaces.
evidence.quote: The process, which essentially involves heating bituminous coal in a closed chamber to remove its volatile material, took about 72 hours.  At the end of the process, the clay seal was broken, and the coke was removed and placed on a train for shipment to an iron furnace in Chattanooga.

evidence.claim: The ovens have sandstone exteriors and firebrick interiors.
evidence.quote: The ovens themselves are 12 feet (3.7 m) in diameter, with sandstone exteriors and firebrick interiors.

evidence.claim: Volunteers helped clear the abandoned site before the park opened in 1987.
evidence.quote: With the help of hundreds of volunteers, the association cleared tons of trash from the area, and the Dunlap Coke Ovens Park opened in 1987.

evidence.claim: Its museum occupies a reconstructed commissary on the original foundation, and a trail follows the incline railway’s grade toward the former mines.
evidence.quote: which it used to reconstruct the commissary on its original foundation.  The reconstructed building now houses the Coke Ovens Museum.

evidence.claim: a trail follows the incline railway’s grade toward the former mines
evidence.quote: A hiking trail now follows the incline railway grade to the former mining areas atop Fredonia Mountain.

evidence.claim: Pikeville’s Old Town Spring supplied the town’s main water source until 1920 and remains visible.
evidence.quote: the Old Town Spring was Pikeville’s main source of water until 1920 and visitors can still see it today.

evidence.claim: The town was established in 1816, and the Bledsoe County seat moved here from Madison by 1818.
evidence.quote: Pikeville was established in 1816 on lands purchased from Charles Love, a land speculator from Virginia.

evidence.claim: U.S. 127 runs through its business district and courthouse square, with a bypass through the newer commercial area to the west.
evidence.quote: In Pikeville, US-127 splits, with the main route running along Main Street through the city's business district and courthouse square, and a bypass running through a newer commercial area in the western part of the city.

evidence.claim: North of town, the highway rises up the mountain near the county line.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 127 heading north out of town as it rises up the mountain near the county line

evidence.claim: Tom Wigle helped build that stretch during a summer job between semesters at Vanderbilt’s engineering school.
evidence.quote: His two sons attended the engineering school at Vanderbilt University. His son Tom (1933–2006) helped build U.S. Route 127 heading north out of town as it rises up the mountain near the county line, during a summer job between semesters at Vanderbilt.

evidence.claim: the Bledsoe County seat moved here from Madison by 1818
evidence.quote: By 1818, the Bledsoe County seat had been moved from Madison to Pikeville.

evidence.claim: The byway organization describes curves and overlooks along the route; the straightness belongs to the valley, not to every mile of highway.
evidence.quote: The Sequatchie Valley National Scenic Byway is a wild and wonderful 70-mile stretch of curves, overlooks, and incredible stops along the route.

evidence.claim: The railcar is located at Whitwell Middle School.
evidence.quote: This rail car is located at the Whitwell Middle School.

evidence.claim: The ruins of the 1906 coal washer are also part of the park.
evidence.quote: the ruins of the 1906 coal washer

evidence.claim: The Sequatchie River passes through the eastern section of town.
evidence.quote: The Sequatchie River passes through the eastern section of Pikeville.

flags: TDOT’s flipbook reverses the valley’s east/west boundaries relative to the valley and Pikeville cache pages. Cardinal assignments omitted.

The driving sheet incorrectly places Jasper at I-40; the Jasper cache places I-24 there. Interstate-start and exit instructions omitted. The sheet and material include Crossville, while the historic-sites page calls Pikeville the northernmost town and Crossville a side trip.
The byway site gives 70 miles; material maps 83.1 miles. Retained the attributed published length without equating it to the mapped distance.

No designation date or original construction history for the entire byway is cached. Overview uses documented corridor travel and Crossville road development without claiming one continuous historic alignment.

Current valley-wall height generalized a roughly 1,000-foot description near Dunlap to the whole valley. Omitted that unsupported scope. The 1805 Cherokee cession is supported by a secondary page but omitted without a treaty or Cherokee source for necessary context.
Dunlap pages disagree on closure in 1922 versus 1927 and name the preservation organization both Society and Association. Omitted closure date and organization name.
Paper-clip totals are presented as memorial contents, not an independently verified count of all Nazi victims. No school access or opening hours are promised.
South-to-north driving order follows the existing moments and official driving sheet, reversing the material strip’s mile numbering.
